<!-- slide · theme coverage -->
## Does the Theme Cover Seaborn & Plotly? {.smaller}

[First plots · setup]{.eyebrow}

### One rule: matplotlib and anything built on it

Your `rcParams` are matplotlib's defaults, so **seaborn inherits them for free**, it draws on matplotlib. The one trap: `sns.set_theme()` overwrites your rcParams with seaborn's grey style, so don't call it (or re-import your theme after).

**Plotly is a different engine** and ignores rcParams completely. You theme it once with a *template*, which `theme.py` registers, so the single import covers all three.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
import seaborn as sns, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import plotly.express as px

# matplotlib + seaborn → inherit rcParams (cream canvas), no styling needed
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 2.2))
sns.barplot(x=["A", "B", "C"], y=[3, 5, 4], ax=ax, color=GREEN)  # seaborn rides on rcParams
ax.set_title("seaborn inherits the theme"); plt.show()

# plotly → needs the template (registered in theme.py)
px.bar(x=["A", "B", "C"], y=[3, 5, 4], template="econ").show()    # matches via template
```


<!-- slide · anatomy intro -->
## Anatomy of a Plot {.smaller}

[First plots · the skeleton]{.eyebrow}

### Every matplotlib plot is the same five lines

Before three libraries, learn the one skeleton they all echo: **import → get data → make a figure → draw → label → show**. Master this and every later plot is a variation on it.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt          # 1. the plotting library
from genomics_course.data import load_timecourse

tc = load_timecourse()                   # 2. get your data (gene, time, tpm, sem)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()                 # 3. fig = whole image, ax = the plot area inside
ax.plot(tc.time, tc.tpm)                 # 4. draw x vs y onto the axes
ax.set_xlabel("time"); ax.set_ylabel("TPM")   # 5. label, then...
plt.show()                               #    ...render it
```


<!-- slide · anatomy step 1 -->
## Anatomy · Step 1 — The Canvas {.smaller}

[First plots · build]{.eyebrow}

### 1 · A figure and an axes

`plt.subplots()` hands back two things: the **figure** (the whole image) and the **axes** (the rectangle you draw inside). Nothing's plotted yet, it's a blank canvas.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "3"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))   # fig = whole image, ax = the area you draw in
plt.show()                                    # empty for now — just the axes
```


<!-- slide · anatomy step 2 -->
## Anatomy · Step 2 — Draw the Data {.smaller}

[First plots · build]{.eyebrow}

### 2 · Put x and y on the axes

Load the data, take one gene to keep it simple, and `ax.plot(x, y)` draws it. `marker="o"` puts a dot at each timepoint so you see the measurements.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "4-5,8"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_timecourse

tc = load_timecourse()                       # gene, time, tpm, sem
one = tc[tc.gene == tc.gene.iloc[0]]          # just the first gene, to start simple

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
ax.plot(one.time, one.tpm, marker="o")       # draw time (x) against expression (y)
plt.show()
```


<!-- slide · anatomy step 3 -->
## Anatomy · Step 3 — Label & Show {.smaller}

[First plots · build]{.eyebrow}

### 3 · Always label; then render

An unlabelled plot is a puzzle. Name the axes, add a title that says what it shows, then `plt.show()`. That's a complete plot, and the template for everything after.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "9-11"
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from genomics_course.data import load_timecourse

tc = load_timecourse()
one = tc[tc.gene == tc.gene.iloc[0]]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
ax.plot(one.time, one.tpm, marker="o")
ax.set_xlabel("time")                        # what the x-axis is
ax.set_ylabel("expression (TPM)")            # what the y-axis is
ax.set_title("One gene over time")           # what the whole plot shows
plt.show()                                    # render it to the slide
```

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Every plot is **figure → axes → draw → label → show**. The next three slides make this exact plot in matplotlib, seaborn, and Plotly, so you'll recognise the same skeleton under each.
:::


<!-- slide · first time series -->
## First Plots · Time Series {.smaller}

[First plots · line]{.eyebrow}

### A gene's expression over time, three ways

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Matplotlib

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
from genomics_course.data import load_timecourse

tc = load_timecourse()                          # gene, time, tpm, sem
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
for g, d in tc.groupby("gene"):                 # one line per gene
    ax.plot(d.time, d.tpm, marker="o", label=g) # connect timepoints
ax.set_xlabel("time"); ax.set_ylabel("TPM")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

### Seaborn

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
import seaborn as sns
from genomics_course.data import load_timecourse

tc = load_timecourse()                          # gene, time, tpm, sem
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
sns.lineplot(tc, x="time", y="tpm", hue="gene", # hue draws one line per gene
             marker="o", ax=ax)
ax.legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

### Plotly

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
import plotly.express as px
from genomics_course.data import load_timecourse

tc = load_timecourse()                          # gene, time, tpm, sem
fig = px.line(tc, x="time", y="tpm", color="gene",  # color = one trace per gene
              markers=True, template="econ")    # template matches the deck
fig.update_layout(height=400)
fig.show()
```

:::

## Exercise · Your First Plot {.smaller}

[First plots · exercise]{.eyebrow}

### Build the skeleton yourself

::: {.exercise}
[Coding exercise]{.xl}
Use the **figure → draw → label → show** skeleton on a new dataset. `load_reads_per_sample()` gives sequencing depth per sample; make a bar chart of it in whichever library you like best.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
from genomics_course.data import load_reads_per_sample

rps = load_reads_per_sample()        # sample, reads

# 1. make a figure:    fig, ax = plt.subplots()
# 2. draw bars:        ax.bar(rps.sample, rps.reads)   (or sns.barplot / px.bar)
# 3. label the y-axis: "reads (millions)"
# 4. add a title that says what the chart shows
# 5. plt.show()   (or fig.show() for plotly)
```
:::

## First Plots · Bar Chart {.smaller}

[First plots · bar]{.eyebrow}

### Expression per tissue, three ways

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Matplotlib

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression()                   # tissue, tpm
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
ax.bar(te.tissue, te.tpm, color=GREEN)          # one bar per tissue
ax.set_ylabel("TPM")
plt.show()
```

### Seaborn

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
import seaborn as sns
from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression()                   # tissue, tpm
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
sns.barplot(te, x="tissue", y="tpm", ax=ax,     # bars straight from the dataframe
            color=GREEN)
plt.show()
```

### Plotly

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
import plotly.express as px
from genomics_course.data import load_tissue_expression

te = load_tissue_expression()                   # tissue, tpm
fig = px.bar(te, x="tissue", y="tpm",           # interactive bars
             template="econ")
fig.update_layout(height=400)
fig.show()
```

:::


<!-- slide · first scatter -->
## First Plots · Scatter {.smaller}

[First plots · scatter]{.eyebrow}

### Co-expression of two genes, three ways

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Matplotlib

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()                        # tissue, gene_x, gene_y
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
for t, d in co.groupby("tissue"):               # colour by tissue (loop)
    ax.scatter(d.gene_x, d.gene_y, label=t, alpha=.7)
ax.set_xlabel("gene X"); ax.set_ylabel("gene Y")
ax.legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

### Seaborn

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
#| fig-width: 5.6
#| fig-height: 4.0
import seaborn as sns
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()                        # tissue, gene_x, gene_y
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
sns.scatterplot(co, x="gene_x", y="gene_y",     # hue colours by tissue automatically
                hue="tissue", alpha=.7, ax=ax)
ax.legend(fontsize=7, frameon=False)
plt.show()
```

### Plotly

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
import plotly.express as px
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()                        # tissue, gene_x, gene_y
fig = px.scatter(co, x="gene_x", y="gene_y",    # hover shows each point
                 color="tissue", template="econ")
fig.update_layout(height=400)
fig.show()
```

:::

## Exercise · Pick Your Library {.smaller}

[First plots · exercise]{.eyebrow}

### Same data, your choice of tool

::: {.exercise}
[Coding exercise]{.xl}
You've now seen all three libraries. Plot the `load_coexpression()` scatter again in the **one library you'd actually reach for**, and add a title that names the relationship. If you pick Plotly, hover a point to read its values.

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
from genomics_course.data import load_coexpression

co = load_coexpression()             # tissue, gene_x, gene_y

# 1. scatter gene_x vs gene_y, coloured by tissue
#    matplotlib (loop) · seaborn (hue=) · or plotly (color=, template="econ")
# 2. title it, e.g. "gene X and gene Y are co-expressed"
# 3. which library felt fastest for this? that's your default from now on
```
:::

::: {.takeaway}
[The bottom line]{.tl}
Same data, three libraries, one identity. **Matplotlib** for control, **seaborn** for one-line statistical plots (both inherit your rcParams), **Plotly** for interactivity (themed by the `econ` template). Reach for the one that fits the job; the look stays constant.
:::
